Particles that are too small risk being evaporated by the laser during the build process, causing issues with powder flow and potentially leading to inclusions and voids in the weld pool. Conversely, particles that are larger than the average particle size can form agglomerates, which negatively affect the flowability of the powder and may lead to surface roughness in as-built parts. Satellites, which occur when small neighboring particles partially fuse to larger particles, can also break off during recoating and contribute to a wider PSD curve. These defects can ultimately lower the density and structural soundness of the material. Figure 2: Formation of smaller particles by recoater. Particle layer packing could be more efficient for recycled powder due to smaller broken particles [17]. A multitude of density and flowability tests are conducted to gain a deeper understanding of the physical characteristics and bulk properties of the powder. These tests are crucial in determining whether a well-packed and uniform powder layer can be achieved across the entire UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 1-3 deposited surface. The importance of well-packed powder cannot be overstated, as it leads to the creation of higher density parts, unhindered by mechanical interlocking friction [4]. Moreover, good powder flowability is a hallmark of a uniformly spread powder with minimal air voids, ensuring that the powder is optimally distributed to produce parts with exceptional quality and consistency. By scrutinizing these properties, manufacturers can unlock the full potential of their powder materials and produce parts that meet the most exacting standards. 1.1.2 Recycling Powder To guarantee the quality and performance of reused powder in LPBF, it is essential to conduct periodic testing of its chemistry composition, PSD, density, flowability, and morphology. This rigorous testing regimen ensures that all powder characteristics remain within acceptable ranges, enabling the powder to behave optimally during the LPBF process. While slight variations in composition may occur after multiple recycling cycles without refreshing, the oxygen content is a notable exception. The increase in oxygen levels can be attributed to various factors, including contaminants, oxidation, vaporization from the powder when exposed to the laser, and handling in ambient air [23-26]. A study by Yusuf et al. on 316L stainless steel, a material closely related to 316H, demonstrated that even after 20 reuse cycles without refreshing, the composition remained within the accepted ran ge specified by the supplier. Furthermore, XRD spectra analysis revealed no phase changes between parts fabricated with virgin and recycled powder, as shown in Figure 3. It is worth noting, however, that the Yusuf et al. research was conducted in a nitrogen environment, which, as an austenite stabilizer, may have suppressed the formation of other phases. Figure 3: (a) 316L composition changes after 20 times recycled, and (b) XRD spectra shows no phase change between virgin and recycled powder [22]. As emphasized in Section 1.1, PSD and powder morphology testing are essential for characterizing recycled powder.
